title: Application of Derivative

notes.heading: 1. Tangents, Normals, Subtangent & Related Rates
notes.proseLatex: At $(x_0, y_0)$ on $y = f(x)$, the tangent slope is $m_T = f'(x_0)$ with equation $y - y_0 = m_T(x - x_0)$, and the normal has slope $m_N = -1/m_T$ (vertical tangent when $1/m_T = 0$). Two curves intersect orthogonally at $P$ if $m_1 m_2 = -1$ at $P$. Related-rate problems differentiate geometric relations (such as $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ or $x^2+y^2=\ell^2$) with respect to time $t$ via the chain rule.

keyFormulas.label: Tangent, Normal & Orthogonal Curves
keyFormulas.latex: $y - y_0 = f'(x_0)(x - x_0),\quad y - y_0 = -\frac{1}{f'(x_0)}(x - x_0),\quad m_1 m_2 = -1 \text{ (orthogonal)}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Write tangent/normal equations and test orthogonal intersection of curves.

examples.problemLatex: Find the slope of the normal to $y = x^3 - 3x + 2$ at $x = 2$.
stepsLatex: Differentiate: $y' = 3x^2 - 3$, so tangent slope at $x=2$ is $m_T = 3(4) - 3 = 9$.

notes.heading: 2. Monotonicity, Concavity & Inflection Points
notes.proseLatex: On an interval $I$, $f'(x) > 0$ implies $f$ is strictly increasing and $f'(x) < 0$ implies $f$ is strictly decreasing (isolated zeros of $f'$ where sign does not flip, such as $x^3$ at $x=0$, preserve strict monotonicity!). Second derivative $f''(x) > 0$ marks upward concavity (convex) and $f''(x) < 0$ marks downward concavity; a point of inflection occurs only where concavity ACTUALLY changes sign across $x_0$.

keyFormulas.label: Monotonicity & Inflection Criterion
keyFormulas.latex: $f'(x) > 0 \implies f \uparrow;\quad f''(x_0)=0 \text{ with sign change of } f'' \implies \text{point of inflection}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Distinguish genuine inflection points from flat fourth-degree minima.

notes.heading: 3. Local vs Global Maxima & Minima
notes.proseLatex: Critical points occur where $f'(c) = 0$ or $f'(c)$ is undefined inside the domain. At a stationary point $f'(c)=0$: $f''(c) < 0$ gives a strict local maximum, $f''(c) > 0$ gives a strict local minimum, and if $f''(c)=0$ one checks the first non-zero higher derivative $f^{(k)}(c)$ (even $k$ gives extremum; odd $k$ gives inflection). On a closed interval $[a,b]$, global extrema MUST compare all interior critical values against the endpoint values $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.

keyFormulas.label: Second Derivative Test & Standard Extrema
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Apply 2nd-derivative test and recall high-frequency JELET extrema.

examples.problemLatex: Find the maximum value of $f(x) = x e^{-x}$ for $x \in [0, \infty)$.
stepsLatex: $f''(x) = e^{-x}(x - 2)$, so $f''(1) = -e^{-1} < 0$ (local & global max on $[0,\infty)$), with $f(1) = \frac{1}{e}$.

wbjeebTraps: $f''(c) = 0$ does NOT automatically mean an inflection point: for $f(x) = x^4$, $f''(0)=0$ yet $x=0$ is a strict minimum.
For $f(x) = x + \frac{1}{x}$ ($x\neq 0$), the local maximum $(-2$ at $x=-1)$ is LESS than the local minimum $(+2$ at $x=1)$ because $x=0$ splits the domain.
On a closed interval $[a,b]$, forgetting to evaluate endpoints $f(a), f(b)$ misses global maxima/minima when $f$ is monotonic.
